Process scheduling is the activity of the operating system that decides which
process runs on the CPU at any given time. Common scheduling algorithms
include First-Come First-Served, Shortest Job First, Round Robin, and
Priority Scheduling. Each algorithm makes different trade-offs between
throughput, latency, and fairness. Round Robin, for example, gives every
process a fixed time quantum and cycles through the ready queue, which
improves fairness and responsiveness for interactive workloads at the cost
of higher average waiting time compared to Shortest Job First when job
lengths vary widely.
